reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: The most common congenital pancreatic ductal variant, in which the dorsal and ventral duct systems fail to fuse
Most of the gland drains through the smaller dorsal duct and minor papilla, with only the ventral duct draining via the major papilla
The great majority of people with pancreas divisum are asymptomatic and it is often an incidental finding

Its causal role in idiopathic recurrent acute pancreatitis is debated, with the prevailing view that it contributes only when combined with additional factors such as a stenotic minor papilla or genetic predisposition
MRCP, ideally with secretin stimulation, is the preferred non-invasive test to demonstrate the separate dorsal duct crossing the bile duct
When intervention is considered in symptomatic recurrent pancreatitis, endoscopic minor papilla sphincterotomy or stenting is the usual approach, with variable and unpredictable benefit
Genetic testing (for example CFTR and SPINK1 variants) is worth considering in young patients with recurrent unexplained pancreatitis
reference.pathophysiology: Pancreas divisum results from failure of the embryonic dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse, so that the bulk of exocrine secretion from the dorsal anlage drains through the accessory (Santorini) duct and the minor papilla, while only the small ventral segment drains through the main (Wirsung) duct and the major papilla. The proposed mechanism for symptoms is relative outflow obstruction: the minor papilla may be too small to accommodate the secretory volume of the dorsal duct, producing raised intraductal pressure, ductal distension, and recurrent pancreatitis in a susceptible minority. Because most individuals with this anatomy never develop symptoms, additional factors such as minor papilla stenosis or genetic susceptibility are thought necessary for clinical disease.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary or genetic pancreatitis (CFTR, SPINK1, PRSS1)
Pancreatic ductal stricture or small neoplasm
additionalInvestigations: MRCP, preferably secretin-enhanced, to demonstrate the dominant dorsal duct and non-union
Endoscopic ultrasound to assess the ducts, parenchyma, and minor papilla
ERCP for definitive ductal anatomy when intervention is planned
Genetic testing for pancreatitis-associated variants in young or recurrent cases
Serum amylase and lipase during episodes to confirm pancreatitis
Fasting triglycerides and calcium to exclude metabolic causes
redFlags: Frequent or severe recurrent attacks of acute pancreatitis
Progression to features of chronic pancreatitis such as ductal changes and exocrine insufficiency
A focal ductal stricture or mass suggesting neoplasm rather than a simple anatomical variant
reference.prognosis: As an isolated anatomical variant the outlook is excellent and no treatment is required; in the minority with recurrent pancreatitis, endoscopic therapy of the minor papilla helps some patients but responses are inconsistent, and a subset progress to chronic pancreatitis.
pitfalls: Assuming the anomaly is the cause of abdominal pain when it is merely an incidental and common finding
Proceeding to endoscopic intervention without objective evidence of recurrent pancreatitis
Overlooking coexisting genetic, metabolic, or biliary causes of recurrent pancreatitis
Underestimating the procedural risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis when intervening on the minor papilla
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Reviews of ductal anatomy and idiopathic recurrent acute pancreatitis
Guidelines on endoscopic management of pancreatic duct anomalies
management: No treatment beyond reassurance for asymptomatic, incidentally discovered pancreas divisum
Standard supportive management of acute pancreatitis episodes with fluids, analgesia and early nutrition
Endoscopic minor papilla sphincterotomy or stenting in selected patients with recurrent acute pancreatitis, acknowledging variable and unpredictable benefit
Investigate and treat co-contributing factors including pancreatitis-associated genetic variants, hypertriglyceridaemia and hypercalcaemia
Alcohol and smoking cessation to reduce the risk of recurrent pancreatitis
Surveillance for progression to chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency
Refer to a hepatobiliary or pancreatology centre for decisions on endoscopic intervention
